clue.text: Formula One driver's car still reaches a hundred

blocks.note: the Jensen is a British sports car, whose name is said the same as the driver's first name
but can mean still or yet, as in 'but even so'
a ton is slang for a hundred, especially a hundred mph

explanation.surface: A racing driver's car still manages to hit a hundred miles an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jensen, a British sports car such as the Interceptor, gives the driver's first name by sound with no signal; 'reaches' simply joins it to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: He is a British racing champion who competed in the top motor-sport series from 2000 onwards.

clue.text: Queen Virginia to be taken on board by military transport - yikes!

indicators.text: to be taken on board by
indicators.note: taking someone on board means carrying them inside, so the royal abbreviation sits within the vehicles

blocks.note: jeeps are army vehicles
ER, Elizabeth Regina
Virginia creeper is a climbing plant, so the state's name suggests the plants

explanation.surface: A queen and a lady called Virginia hitch a ride on an army truck, to everyone's alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: Virginia is not VA here: it stands for the second word by way of the Virginia creeper, a garden climber.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise or fright, just like the interjection given.

clue.text: Approaching the time which is said to fall

blocks.note: nigh means near or approaching
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone senses the hour is near when something will come down.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole closing phrase: darkness is conventionally said to fall.
explanation.definitionFit: We speak of darkness falling at evening, so the dark hours are the thing commonly said to fall.

clue.text: Implement to carve ham

indicators.note: to implement is to put into working effect, so the following letters are worked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook reaches for a knife to slice a joint of ham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implement' looks like a noun for a knife, and ham like meat; both are switched, ham being a verb for hammy acting.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham is to perform in an exaggerated, theatrical way, which is exactly what this verb means.

clue.text: Is one picky as Patton?

indicators.note: the question mark invites the solver to rearrange the general's surname rather than read it literally

blocks.note: the American general's surname, taken as letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person is as fussy as General Patton.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase meaning 'one who chooses', bent to fit the question form of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An optant is someone who exercises an option or makes a choice, so a person who picks.

clue.text: Saw dog in pub, gutless

indicators.note: with its guts removed the word keeps only its outside letters
the dog sits inside the bar, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the first and last letters of pub
Rover is the stock name for a dog

explanation.surface: A drinker reports spotting a scrawny hound in the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw looks like the past tense of see; here it is the noun for an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional saying or maxim, the same thing as an adage passed down the generations.

clue.text: Abhorrence of pain that varies, variable

indicators.note: something that varies changes its form, so these letters change their order

blocks.note: taken as written
in algebra x, y and z are the usual variables

explanation.surface: A sufferer loathes a pain that comes and goes unpredictably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain that' is only fodder; 'that' does double duty in the surface but simply supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipathy is a deep-seated dislike or aversion, close in meaning to loathing or abhorrence.

clue.text: Old instrument needs the sphere to ring

blocks.note: taken as written
an orb is a sphere
the letter O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: An antique instrument apparently requires a globe before it will sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The theorbo is a large bass lute used in the seventeenth century, an early stringed instrument.

clue.text: A quarter invested in bags of crisps, say

indicators.note: something invested in a thing is put into it, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: sacks are large bags
north is one of the four compass quarters

explanation.surface: A quarter of something is put inside packets of potato crisps.
explanation.walkthrough: A quarter is a compass point here, not a fraction; crisps are what Americans call potato chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Crisps are a typical light bite between meals, given as an example of small eats.

clue.text: Song about to catch flies

blocks.note: surface reading: a tune about trapping insects
setter's reading: a children's counting song whose title names a kind of fly, and a bottle can be used to trap flies

explanation.surface: Somebody hums a ditty while trying to swat insects.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is a British children's counting song in which bottles fall off a wall one by one; a greenbottle is also a common blowfly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a well-known nursery counting song, sung while counting down the number of items on a wall.

clue.text: Bed for a big girl

blocks.note: a berth is a bed on a ship or train
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop advertises a bed suitable for a large young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Bertha was the nickname of a huge German gun in the First World War, and the name stuck to anything outsized.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase Big Bertha makes this female name the stock label for something or someone very large.

clue.text: See 1 down
A distressed call for installation of the greatest domestic hazard?

indicators.note: installing something means fitting it inside, so one piece is set within the distress signal

blocks.note: taken as written
the international distress signal
the best is the greatest

explanation.surface: A panicked phone call about the best possible kitchen fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: old houses often have this fibrous material in their walls and ceilings.
explanation.definitionFit: This fireproof mineral, once used in building insulation, is a cancer risk found in many older homes.

clue.text: Dreadful tune during further performance cut short by fight

indicators.note: a dreadful tune is a mangled one, so its letters are jumbled
cutting something short trims off its final letter
one thing happening during another lies inside it

blocks.note: an encore is an extra performance demanded by the audience
taken as written

explanation.surface: A terrible song played as an encore is interrupted by a scuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: The trimmed encore loses its last E before the jumbled tune is slipped in after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter can be a hostile meeting or clash, such as a skirmish between armed forces.

clue.text: See 1
Carriage provided to go round the area

indicators.note: going round means turning about, so the short word is read backwards

blocks.note: provided that means if
an acre is a unit of area

explanation.surface: A coach is laid on for a tour of the district.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiacre is a small four-wheeled hackney coach once common in Paris, a horse-drawn vehicle for hire.

clue.text: Piece of hip music hip? Virtually swinging!

indicators.note: virtually means almost entirely, so the word loses its final letter
swinging things move about freely, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the second hip in the clue, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a fragment of trendy swing music counts as cool.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'hip' is anatomical and part of the definition; the second is only fodder, trimmed to two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The ischium is the curved bone forming the lower rear part of each side of the pelvis.

clue.text: Nothing to interest me about the interdict

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the whole phrase is read backwards

blocks.note: O looks like zero
to grab someone is to catch their interest
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that the ban leaves them completely cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The informal 'does it grab me?' supplies the middle; the three pieces are joined and the lot is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official prohibition, especially on trade, just as an interdict is an authoritative ban.

clue.text: Steer to the right of me, by no mistake: change here?

indicators.note: a mistake is an error, so the preceding letters are set down in the wrong order
in a horizontal answer what lies to the right comes after, fixing the order of the pieces

blocks.note: taken as written
a steer is a castrated bull, an ox

explanation.surface: Driving instructions: bear right, and no mistakes, as things change here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' reads as a verb for driving, but it is the animal; 'change' is loose coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose coins are saved in this container, so it is where small change is kept, hinted by the question mark.

clue.text: Formula One enthusiast turned eccentric has to take hint - one is rambling

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the word for eccentric is read backwards

blocks.note: rum is an old British word for odd or peculiar
a ray, as in a ray of hope, is a faint trace or hint
someone who is rambling is out on a hike

explanation.surface: A motor-racing fan has gone peculiar and must be reminded of something, as he rambles on.
explanation.walkthrough: Murray Walker was the BBC's famously excitable Formula One commentator; 'rambling' is a nod to his torrents of commentary as well as the walking.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a commentator famous for his breathless love of motor racing, the sport's best-known fan in Britain.

clue.text: Now Epiphany, as if any were needed

definitions.note: Epiphany, 6 January, falls in the opening days of this period

indicators.note: needed puns on kneaded, and dough that is kneaded is worked into a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that Epiphany has come round, as though anyone wanted it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needed' is the anagram signal only through its twin 'kneaded'. Epiphany on 6 January marks the start of the calendar, so it is now this season.
explanation.definitionFit: Epiphany falls on 6 January, so when it arrives we are in the opening days of the calendar's fresh twelve months.

clue.text: Nothing orange about this plant!

indicators.note: about can mean moved around, so the fruit's letters are shuffled

blocks.note: O looks like zero
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener insists this herb has no citrus about it whatsoever.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface claims there is no orange in the plant, yet all six letters of the fruit are in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic herb of the mint family, a plant used widely in Mediterranean cooking.

clue.text: With which to purify floozie?

blocks.note: first meaning: a brush or device for cleaning things
second meaning: British slang for a promiscuous woman

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is coarse British slang; the first is the plain tool that cleans by rubbing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a cleaning brush or gas-cleaning apparatus and, as slang, a loose or disreputable woman.

clue.text: See 18 down
Compare growth in conversation

indicators.note: in conversation means as spoken, so we hear the word rather than spell it

blocks.note: lichen is a crusty growth on rocks and trees

explanation.surface: Two people discuss and weigh up how much something has grown.
explanation.definitionFit: To liken one thing to another is to point out their similarity, the same as comparing them.

clue.text: Posh (with a plum) should be given the nod to put meat on

blocks.note: the Victoria is a well-known variety of plum
a beck is a beckoning nod or gesture, as in at someone's beck and call
ham is a meat

explanation.surface: Someone posh, with a plum in her mouth, should be allowed to fatten up a little.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh Spice of the Spice Girls is the stage name of this singer; a plum in the mouth is a cut-glass accent.
explanation.definitionFit: She performed as Posh Spice in the pop group, so the single word is her famous nickname.

clue.text: Actor wearing fertiliser to make love

blocks.note: marl is a clay-rich soil spread as fertiliser
clothes being worn are on
a make is a brand of goods
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A performer covered in manure tries to seduce someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make love' looks like a single phrase, but it splits into a noun for a manufacturer's label and the tennis score.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the celebrated American film star of On the Waterfront and The Godfather.
